fields.features_heading: What the Form Asks Before It Names a Price
fields.features_subheading: These six pieces turn a customer's answers into a price, or into a site walk when the job is too big to price from a form.
fields.feature_1:
A price that follows the rooms

Set a base price for each home size and a step for every extra bathroom. The form does the math as the customer answers and shows the price per visit before anyone submits.
fields.feature_2:
Rates tied to the cleaning schedule

Offer weekly, every-two-weeks, and monthly visits at their own rates. When the customer picks a schedule, the total on screen changes to the per-visit rate for that choice.
fields.feature_3:
Extras priced one at a time

List add-ons such as inside the oven or interior windows, each with its own price and checkbox. Every extra the customer ticks is added to the quote total on screen.
fields.feature_4:
Large jobs held for a site walk

Pick the square footage where a form price stops being safe. A request over that line shows no price and goes on the owner's list for a site walk, with the address attached.
fields.feature_5:
Each request in an email or Slack

Choose who hears about a new request and where: an email to the owner or a post in a Slack channel. The message carries the address and the total the customer saw on screen.
fields.feature_6:
Code you can take to your own site

On paid plans, export the full code to your GitHub repository. A developer can then place the quote form inside an existing booking site and keep building on it there.

fields.usecase_heading: How Four Cleaning Jobs Get Quoted
fields.tab_content_1:
Three bedrooms, every two weeks: $135 a visit

Kalinda Vaszary wants her house with 3 bedrooms and 2 bathrooms cleaned every two weeks. Vellacott Home Cleaning's form prices that home at $150 for a standard clean and takes 10% off for the every-two-weeks schedule. She sees $135 a visit before she submits, and her request is saved with her answers.
fields.tab_content_2:
Oven, fridge, and windows lift a move-out to $330

Corban Mirelli hands back the keys to his 1-bedroom apartment on May 29. On Blumquist Cleaning Co.'s form he picks a move-out clean at $220 and ticks three extras: inside the oven for $35, inside the fridge for $30, and interior windows for $45. An email gives him the $330 quote and his move-out date.
fields.tab_content_3:
Two cabins, 14 July checkouts, and one $1,330 quote

Ottaline Zelenka rents out 2 cabins and expects 14 checkouts in July. Granfield Turnover Cleaning's form asks for the cabins, the checkout count, and whether linens are included. It prices 14 turnovers at $95 each, $1,330 for the month, and posts the request to the #turnovers channel in Slack.
fields.tab_content_4:
Ardmoor's new build gets walked before it gets priced

Ardmoor Builders has a 4,800-square-foot house ready for its final clean and asks Merriday Cleaning for a quote. Anything over 4,000 square feet gets a site walk before a price, and the form shows no total. The request goes on the owner's list marked Site walk needed, next to 2 smaller jobs already priced.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Cleaning Quote Form
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to build a cleaning quote form that totals each home on screen and sends large jobs to a site walk.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Write down the jobs you turn down
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Price one recent home by hand
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Ask only what changes the price
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Name who books each site walk
fields.howto_step_1_des: List the cleaning you take on and the cleaning you refuse, such as biohazard cleanup or hoarding work. Put that list in the first question of the form. A customer whose job is outside it finds out before typing an address or a phone number.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Pick a job from last month, such as a 2-bedroom condo cleaned weekly, and write out how you reached the price. The base rate, each extra bathroom, and the schedule discount become the form's rules. The form should land on your number.
fields.howto_step_3_des: The size of the home and the visit schedule belong on the form, because each one moves the total. Leave off anything you can learn at the door. Then fill the form on a phone yourself and cut any question that does not change the total.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Decide who visits the jobs your form will not price, and how soon they reply. Give that person a target, such as one business day, and a backup for weekends. Put both names in the prompt so these requests reach them.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Put your prices and the site-walk rule into one prompt. Emergent builds the form, the database behind it, and the logic that totals each quote. When a price changes next season, ask for the new number in plain English and the form updates.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Send recurring requests to whoever schedules the regular crews and one-time jobs to the owner. A Slack channel suits a team that shares the work, and an email suits one person. Include the total the customer saw in every message.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Request a small apartment, a large house with every extra, and a home over your site-walk line. Check each total against your own math. Then confirm the large request showed no price and reached the person who books site walks.

faq_plan.q: What is a cleaning quote form?
faq_plan.a: A cleaning quote form is the request a cleaning business puts on its website so customers can ask for a price. It collects the size of the home or building and the type of clean wanted. The answers either produce a price on screen or give the owner what they need to send one.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a cleaning quote form?
faq_plan.a: Write down your prices first: the base rate by home size and every extra. Then describe the form and those prices to Emergent's AI form builder. It builds the form and the database behind it, and any price can be changed later by asking.

faq_plan.q: What questions should a cleaning quote form ask?
faq_plan.a: Ask what sets the price. Start with the type of clean and the size of the home, then the visit schedule and any extras. Add the address and a phone number last. Hold questions about parking or door codes until the booking, since those answers change nothing on the quote.

faq_plan.q: How should a cleaning quote form handle commercial cleaning requests?
faq_plan.a: Give commercial work its own branch of questions. Ask for the square footage, the number of restrooms, the cleaning days each week, and the hours the building is empty. If a facility manager sends its own rfp form instead, answer it with the same rates your form uses. Both quotes then agree.

faq_plan.q: Should a cleaning quote form show an exact price or a range?
faq_plan.a: Show an exact price when the answers describe the whole job, such as a recurring clean of a home with known rooms. Show a range, or no price, when the condition of the space decides the work, as with a first deep clean. Say on the form that the final price is confirmed at the first visit.

faq_plan.q: How do I add extras like inside the oven to a cleaning quote form?
faq_plan.a: Give each extra its own checkbox and a flat price, then let the form add the ones the customer ticks. Price each one from the time it takes your crew. Show the running total beside the list. The customer then sees what every extra adds before submitting.

faq_plan.q: What happens after a customer submits a cleaning quote form?
faq_plan.a: The app saves the request with every answer and its quoted price, then emails the owner or posts in Slack. For a contract cleaning job, follow up with a proposal form that sets out the scope and the terms. With Emergent, each request lands in a database you own.

faq_plan.q: How long should a cleaning quote form be?
faq_plan.a: Keep it to the questions that move the price, which for a house clean is five to seven. Group them by topic, with the home first, then the schedule, then the extras. Forms built with Emergent have no response caps.

faq_plan.q: When should a cleaning quote form ask for a walkthrough instead of giving a price?
faq_plan.a: Ask for one whenever the answers cannot tell you the condition of the space. Post-construction work and a first deep clean in months both fit. Put a short notes box beside those choices for the customer to describe the space before the visit.

faq_plan.q: What should a cleaning quote form ask about a one-time event?
faq_plan.a: Ask for the event date and the guest count, then whether you clean before the event or after it. Add a separate line for late-night work after the event ends. If the organizer offers sponsorship credit in place of payment, ask for their sponsorship form and weigh its value against your quote.

plan.angle: The search has almost no volume and no ranked top 10 in the workbook, so the page wins on usefulness: template pages for this query stop at name, address and a notes box, which leaves the cleaner to call back and ask the size of the home. This page shows the questions that actually set a cleaning price (bedrooms, bathrooms, frequency, extras, square footage) across four kinds of cleaning work: a recurring house clean priced on screen, a move-out clean with priced extras, vacation rental turnovers counted per month, and post-construction cleanup that sends large sites to a walkthrough instead of a guess. The FAQ covers the definition, building one, the fields to ask, commercial requests, price versus range, extras, what happens after submit, length, residential and commercial in one form, and one-time event cleaning.
